summary:
Crew Health is a health monitor astronauts run on themselves during long missions. Each flight day starts with a
short, required check-in: vital signs, sleep and mood, symptoms, food, water and exercise, and radiation dose. The
app compares every reading with the astronaut's own pre-flight baseline and shows the result on a scan-style body map:
the organ or bone that needs attention lights up in place, yellow for caution and red for warning. Opening a system
explains what space does to it and what to do today, in sentences quoted from NASA's Human Research Program and the
Canadian Space Agency. Weekly and monthly checks catch symptoms that keep coming back and values that drift slowly,
and anything at warning is written to a simulated ground link. Far from Earth, where help can be up to 20 minutes away
one way, the crew has to notice its own health changes; Crew Health turns NASA's description of those changes into
a daily routine and a picture anyone can read at a glance.
details:
**What it does**

**Body map.** Twelve body systems on one scan-style figure: brain, mind and sleep; eyes; inner ear and balance; heart and vessels; lungs and oxygen; blood and immunity; bones; spine; muscles; digestion and nutrition; kidneys; and radiation for the whole body. A flagged system lights up where it is in the body. Status is always shown three ways at once: colour, shape (circle, triangle, square) and a word (nominal, caution, warning).

**Daily check-in.** Five required steps. Until they are done, the other screens stay locked. Each field says what the measurement is, how to take it, and why NASA tracks it, with a link to the source page.

**Status against your own baseline.** Readings are compared with the astronaut's pre-flight values. The status follows 3-day averages and 7-day totals so that one bad night does not raise an alarm; today's value is shown next to the average.

**Long-term checks.** Weekly and monthly reviews flag a symptom that keeps coming back (3 of the last 7 days, or 10 of the last 30), a value outside its limit on 15 or more of the last 30 days, and a value that drifts further from baseline week after week.

**Critical readings.** A single reading far from baseline asks the astronaut to measure again or confirm it; a confirmed one is reported to the ground at once.

**Symptom check.** At any time the astronaut can report what they notice. The app asks about the other signs of the conditions it may belong to and for the measurements that help tell them apart, then answers that question first.

**Possible conditions, never a diagnosis.** Findings are matched with 17 conditions the NASA and CSA pages describe and named as "Possible: …" with the source sentence. When only a habit points to a condition (too little water or exercise), the app says "Risk: …" instead.

**What to do.** Each system lists the countermeasures the sources give, as tick-boxes that go into today's plan.

**Simulated ground link.** Urgent findings, confirmed critical readings, weekly and monthly reviews and missed check-ins become messages in a ground log, with the mission's communication delay. Nothing leaves the device.

**Missions.** Station (180 days), Moon (30 days, the team's setting) and Mars (about three years, up to 20 minutes one way), each emphasising different hazards.

**Weekly tests.** A reaction-time test and a tumbling-E vision test on screen. They are not clinical tests: they compare the astronaut with their own baseline.

**How it works**

The app is a web application written in TypeScript with React, built with Vite. It needs no server and no network: data stays in the device's local storage. It also runs as a Windows program (Electron), installed or as a single file. The health content lives in data files separate from the code. Every health sentence carries a source page and a verbatim quote, and an automated test fails if a quote is not found word for word in the saved copy of its page.

The project has 524 automated tests (Vitest and Testing Library).

The source pages give no normal ranges or alert limits for vital signs. Every limit in the app is the team's own setting; the app says so next to every status and lists all limits on its Sources screen.

**Benefits and goal**

On a long mission the crew carries much of the responsibility for spotting changes in themselves. Crew Health gives them a daily routine that takes a few minutes, a picture of the whole body that reads at a glance, and advice that is traceable to NASA's own words. Our goal was a tool an astronaut could trust because it never says more than its

sources do.

**Tools, languages and software**

TypeScript, React, Vite, Vitest, Testing Library, Electron, electron-builder, Node.js. Fonts: Instrument Sans and Martian Mono (SIL Open Font License). All demo data is simulated and labelled as such on every screen.
